name: Jebel Irhoud
what: Skulls and teeth from a cave in Morocco, dated about 315,000 years ago, have a modern face and an older, longer braincase.
why: The oldest known Homo sapiens: our species was already spread across Africa, not born in one East African valley.

sources.cite: Hublin, J.-J. et al., "New fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco and the pan-African origin of Homo sapiens", Nature 546, 289-292 (2017)
Richter, D. et al., "The age of the hominin fossils from Jebel Irhoud, Morocco", Nature 546, 293-296 (2017)

name: Kabwe (Broken Hill)
what: A heavy-browed skull found in a Zambian mine, redated in 2020 to about 299,000 years ago.
why: Several kinds of human lived in Africa at once when our species appeared.

sources.cite: Grün, R. et al., "Dating the skull from Broken Hill, Zambia, and its position in human evolution", Nature 580, 372-375 (2020)

name: Rising Star Cave
what: Over 1,500 bones of Homo naledi, a small-brained human, deep in a South African cave system.
why: A species with a brain a third the size of ours lived alongside early Homo sapiens.

sources.cite: Dirks, P. et al., "The age of Homo naledi and associated sediments in the Rising Star Cave, South Africa", eLife 6, e24231 (2017)

name: Florisbad
what: A partial skull from a spring mound in the Free State, about 259,000 years old.
why: An early member of our lineage in southern Africa.

sources.cite: Grün, R. et al., "Direct dating of Florisbad hominid", Nature 382, 500-501 (1996)

name: Omo Kibish
what: Omo I, found by Richard Leakey in 1967, lies under ash from a 233,000-year-old eruption.
why: The oldest Homo sapiens from East Africa, dated by the volcano that buried it.

sources.cite: Vidal, C. M. et al., "Age of the oldest known Homo sapiens from eastern Africa", Nature 601, 579-583 (2022)

name: Apidima Cave
what: A skull fragment from southern Greece read as Homo sapiens, about 210,000 years old; disputed.
why: If right, modern humans reached Europe 150,000 years before they stayed.

sources.cite: Harvati, K. et al., "Apidima Cave fossils provide earliest evidence of Homo sapiens in Eurasia", Nature 571, 500-504 (2019)

name: Misliya Cave
what: An upper jaw on Mount Carmel, Israel, dated 194,000 to 177,000 years ago.
why: Modern humans were leaving Africa long before the main dispersal; these early groups left no living descendants we can detect.

sources.cite: Hershkovitz, I. et al., "The earliest modern humans outside Africa", Science 359, 456-459 (2018)

name: Pinnacle Point
what: Shellfish meals and ground red ochre in a cave above the sea on the South African coast.
why: The earliest known seafood diet and pigment use: coasts may have been refuges in a harsh glacial stage.

sources.cite: Marean, C. W. et al., "Early human use of marine resources and pigment in South Africa during the Middle Pleistocene", Nature 449, 905-908 (2007)

name: Qafzeh and Skhul
what: Modern humans buried with ochre and shells in two caves in Israel, 120,000 to 90,000 years ago.
why: A wave out of Africa during a wet, warm spell; later the Levant was Neanderthal country again.

sources.cite: Valladas, H. et al., "Thermoluminescence dating of Mousterian Proto-Cro-Magnon remains from Israel and the origin of modern man", Nature 331, 614-616 (1988)
Grün, R. et al., "U-series and ESR analyses of bones and teeth relating to the human burials from Skhul", Journal of Human Evolution 49, 316-334 (2005)

name: Ngandong
what: A bone bed on the Solo River in Java with the last known Homo erectus, 117,000 to 108,000 years ago.
why: Homo erectus lasted over a million years; it died out here as the forest closed in.

sources.cite: Rizal, Y. et al., "Last appearance of Homo erectus at Ngandong, Java, 117,000-108,000 years ago", Nature 577, 381-385 (2020)

name: Blombos Cave
what: Ochre engraved with cross-hatching and a drawing in ochre crayon on a stone flake, about 73,000 years old.
why: The oldest known drawing: symbolic thinking well before Europe's painted caves.

sources.cite: Henshilwood, C. S. et al., "Emergence of modern human behavior: Middle Stone Age engravings from South Africa", Science 295, 1278-1280 (2002)
Henshilwood, C. S. et al., "An abstract drawing from the 73,000-year-old levels at Blombos Cave, South Africa", Nature 562, 115-118 (2018)

name: Panga ya Saidi
what: A child of about three, laid on its side in a pit with its head on a pillow: "Mtoto".
why: The oldest known human burial in Africa.

sources.cite: Martinón-Torres, M. et al., "Earliest known human burial in Africa", Nature 593, 95-100 (2021)

name: Shanidar Cave
what: Ten Neanderthals in a cave in Iraqi Kurdistan, some buried; one, Shanidar 1, lived for years with crippling injuries.
why: Neanderthals cared for the injured and may have buried their dead (the "flower burial" pollen is disputed).

sources.cite: Pomeroy, E. et al., "New Neanderthal remains associated with the 'flower burial' at Shanidar Cave", Antiquity 94, 11-26 (2020)

name: Diepkloof Rock Shelter
what: Ostrich eggshell water flasks engraved with repeating patterns, 65,000 to 55,000 years ago.
why: A shared graphic tradition: people marked their belongings the way groups mark identity.

sources.cite: Texier, P.-J. et al., "A Howiesons Poort tradition of engraving ostrich eggshell containers dated to 60,000 years ago at Diepkloof Rock Shelter", PNAS 107, 6180-6185 (2010)

name: Denisova Cave
what: A cave in the Altai with a finger bone that gave the first Denisovan genome, and "Denny", a girl with a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father.
why: Three kinds of human used this cave; they met and had children.

sources.cite: Reich, D. et al., "Genetic history of an archaic hominin group from Denisova Cave in Siberia", Nature 468, 1053-1060 (2010)
Slon, V. et al., "The genome of the offspring of a Neanderthal mother and a Denisovan father", Nature 561, 113-116 (2018)
Jacobs, Z. et al., "Timing of archaic hominin occupation of Denisova Cave in southern Siberia", Nature 565, 594-599 (2019)

name: Baishiya Karst Cave
what: A Denisovan jaw from a monks' cave 3,280 m up on the Tibetan Plateau, at least 160,000 years old.
why: Denisovans lived at altitude; Tibetans today carry a Denisovan gene (EPAS1) that helps them breathe thin air.

sources.cite: Chen, F. et al., "A late Middle Pleistocene Denisovan mandible from the Tibetan Plateau", Nature 569, 409-412 (2019)

name: Tam Pà Ling
what: A modern human skull and jaw from a cave in northern Laos, 86,000 to 68,000 years old.
why: Modern humans may have reached mainland Southeast Asia before the main wave out of Africa.

sources.cite: Freidline, S. E. et al., "Early presence of Homo sapiens in Southeast Asia by 86-68 kyr at Tam Pà Ling, Northern Laos", Nature Communications 14, 3193 (2023)

name: Liang Bua
what: Skeletons of Homo floresiensis, the "hobbit", about a metre tall, on the island of Flores.
why: An island dwarf human that lived until about 60,000 years ago; its stone tools stop about 50,000 years ago, near when modern humans came.

sources.cite: Sutikna, T. et al., "Revised stratigraphy and chronology for Homo floresiensis at Liang Bua in Indonesia", Nature 532, 366-369 (2016)

name: Callao Cave
what: Teeth and bones of a new small human, Homo luzonensis, on Luzon in the Philippines.
why: Another island human: archaic people crossed the sea to the Philippines long before us.

sources.cite: Détroit, F. et al., "A new species of Homo from the Late Pleistocene of the Philippines", Nature 568, 181-186 (2019)

name: Madjedbebe
what: Stone axes, grindstones and ochre in a rock shelter in Arnhem Land, dated to about 65,000 years ago.
why: Either the first Australians arrived 65,000 years ago or about 50,000; the dates are argued over.

sources.cite: Clarkson, C. et al., "Human occupation of northern Australia by 65,000 years ago", Nature 547, 306-310 (2017)
O'Connell, J. F. et al., "When did Homo sapiens first reach Southeast Asia and Sahul?", PNAS 115, 8482-8490 (2018)

debate.view: Closer to 50,000 years ago; the artefacts may have moved down through the sand

name: Grotte Mandrin
what: A child's tooth and tiny stone points in a Rhône valley rock shelter sandwiched between Neanderthal layers.
why: Modern humans visited France about 54,000 years ago, 10,000 years before they stayed; then Neanderthals returned.

sources.cite: Slimak, L. et al., "Modern human incursion into Neanderthal territories 54,000 years ago at Mandrin, France", Science Advances 8, eabj9496 (2022)

name: Leang Karampuang
what: A painted scene of three human-like figures with a wild pig, at least 51,200 years old, in a Sulawesi cave.
why: The oldest known figurative art and the oldest known story told in pictures.

sources.cite: Oktaviana, A. A. et al., "Narrative cave art in Indonesia by 51,200 years ago", Nature 631, 814-818 (2024)

name: Ranis (Ilsenhöhle)
what: Bone scraps under a castle in Thuringia, identified as modern human by DNA, about 47,000 years old.
why: Small groups of modern humans lived in a cold steppe in central Europe while Neanderthals were still there.

sources.cite: Mylopotamitaki, D. et al., "Homo sapiens reached the higher latitudes of Europe by 45,000 years ago", Nature 626, 341-346 (2024)

name: Bacho Kiro Cave
what: Modern human bones, pendants of cave-bear teeth and stone blades in a Bulgarian cave, 46,000 to 43,000 years ago.
why: Some of these people had a Neanderthal ancestor only a few generations back.

sources.cite: Hublin, J.-J. et al., "Initial Upper Palaeolithic Homo sapiens from Bacho Kiro Cave, Bulgaria", Nature 581, 299-302 (2020)

name: Ust'-Ishim
what: A thigh bone washed out of a riverbank in western Siberia gave the oldest modern human genome.
why: His DNA dates the Neanderthal mixing to 50,000 to 60,000 years ago.

sources.cite: Fu, Q. et al., "Genome sequence of a 45,000-year-old modern human from western Siberia", Nature 514, 445-449 (2014)

name: Peștera cu Oase
what: A jaw in a Romanian cave whose owner had a Neanderthal ancestor four to six generations back.
why: Direct proof that modern humans and Neanderthals had children in Europe.

sources.cite: Fu, Q. et al., "An early modern human from Romania with a recent Neanderthal ancestor", Nature 524, 216-219 (2015)

name: Hohle Fels and Hohlenstein-Stadel
what: Caves in the Swabian Jura with the Lion Man, a Venus figurine and bone flutes, about 40,000 years old.
why: The oldest known figurines and musical instruments.

sources.cite: Conard, N. J., "A female figurine from the basal Aurignacian of Hohle Fels Cave in southwestern Germany", Nature 459, 248-252 (2009)

name: Tianyuan Cave
what: A modern human near Beijing about 40,000 years old; his DNA links him to later East Asians and Native Americans.
why: East Asia's population history goes back at least this far.

sources.cite: Fu, Q. et al., "DNA analysis of an early modern human from Tianyuan Cave, China", PNAS 110, 2223-2227 (2013)

name: Gorham's Cave
what: A sea cave on Gibraltar with Neanderthal hearths and an engraved hashtag on the floor.
why: Among the last Neanderthal refuges; how late they lasted here is argued over.

sources.cite: Finlayson, C. et al., "Late survival of Neanderthals at the southernmost extreme of Europe", Nature 443, 850-853 (2006)
Higham, T. et al., "The timing and spatiotemporal patterning of Neanderthal disappearance", Nature 512, 306-309 (2014)

debate.view: Neanderthals lasted here until about 28,000 years ago
They were gone everywhere by about 40,000 years ago

name: Sungir
what: Graves near Vladimir with two children and a man dressed in thousands of mammoth-ivory beads.
why: Ice Age foragers lived in small, far-flung networks that avoided marrying close kin.

sources.cite: Sikora, M. et al., "Ancient genomes show social and reproductive behavior of early Upper Paleolithic foragers", Science 358, 659-662 (2017)

name: Yana Rhinoceros Horn Site
what: Mammoth hunters camped above the Arctic Circle in Siberia, 32,000 years ago.
why: People coped with the far north before the Last Glacial Maximum; their kin later reached Beringia.

sources.cite: Pitulko, V. V. et al., "The Yana RHS site: humans in the Arctic before the Last Glacial Maximum", Science 303, 52-56 (2004)

name: Dolní Věstonice
what: A camp of mammoth hunters in Moravia with the oldest fired-clay figurine, the Venus of Dolní Věstonice.
why: People fired clay 15,000 years before anyone made pots from it.

sources.cite: Vandiver, P. B. et al., "The origins of ceramic technology at Dolní Věstonice, Czechoslovakia", Science 246, 1002-1008 (1989)

name: Mal'ta
what: A boy buried near Lake Baikal with ivory birds and a necklace; his genome is a third Native American.
why: One Siberian population was ancestral both to Europeans and to the first Americans.

sources.cite: Raghavan, M. et al., "Upper Palaeolithic Siberian genome reveals dual ancestry of Native Americans", Nature 505, 87-91 (2014)

name: Ohalo II
what: Brush huts by the Sea of Galilee with wild wheat and barley, sickle blades and weeds of cultivated fields.
why: Trial cultivation 11,000 years before farming took hold.

sources.cite: Snir, A. et al., "The origin of cultivation and proto-weeds, long before Neolithic farming", PLoS ONE 10, e0131422 (2015)

name: White Sands footprints
what: Human footprints, many of children, beside a lake in New Mexico, dated 23,000 to 21,000 years ago.
why: If right, people were in the Americas during the Last Glacial Maximum, thousands of years earlier than once thought.

sources.cite: Bennett, M. R. et al., "Evidence of humans in North America during the Last Glacial Maximum", Science 373, 1528-1531 (2021)
Pigati, J. S. et al., "Independent age estimates resolve the controversy of ancient human footprints at White Sands", Science 382, 73-75 (2023)

name: Xianrendong Cave
what: Pottery sherds 20,000 years old in a cave in Jiangxi, China.
why: Foragers cooked in pots 10,000 years before farming: pottery did not need farmers.

sources.cite: Wu, X. et al., "Early pottery at 20,000 years ago in Xianrendong Cave, China", Science 336, 1696-1700 (2012)

name: Monte Verde
what: A camp of wooden huts by a creek in southern Chile, preserved in peat, 14,500 years old.
why: People reached the far south of the Americas before the ice-free corridor opened, so they likely came down the coast.

sources.cite: Dillehay, T. D. et al., "Monte Verde: seaweed, food, medicine, and the peopling of South America", Science 320, 784-786 (2008)

name: Paisley Caves
what: Human coprolites with DNA in Oregon caves, 14,300 years old.
why: Pre-Clovis people in the far west of North America.

sources.cite: Gilbert, M. T. P. et al., "DNA from pre-Clovis human coprolites in Oregon, North America", Science 320, 786-789 (2008)

name: Bonn-Oberkassel
what: A man and a woman buried with a young dog that had been nursed through distemper.
why: The oldest undisputed domestic dog, cared for by its people.

sources.cite: Janssens, L. et al., "A new look at an old dog: Bonn-Oberkassel reconsidered", Journal of Archaeological Science 92, 126-138 (2018)

name: Blackwater Draw (Clovis)
what: Fluted Clovis spear points with mammoth bones near Clovis, New Mexico.
why: Clovis spread across North America within a few centuries; it is no longer thought to be the first culture there.

sources.cite: Waters, M. R. & Stafford, T. W., "Redefining the age of Clovis: implications for the peopling of the Americas", Science 315, 1122-1126 (2007)

name: Star Carr
what: A lakeside camp in Yorkshire with the oldest known house in Britain and red-deer antler headdresses.
why: Britain was still joined to Europe by Doggerland when people built here.

sources.cite: Milner, N. et al., Star Carr Volume 1: A Persistent Place in a Changing World (White Rose University Press, 2018)

name: Jiahu
what: A Neolithic village in Henan with rice, bone flutes still playable, and fermented drinks.
why: Early farming villages in China, with music.

sources.cite: Zhang, J. et al., "Oldest playable musical instruments found at Jiahu early Neolithic site in China", Nature 401, 366-368 (1999)

name: Lepenski Vir
what: Trapezoid houses and fish-faced sandstone heads by the Iron Gates of the Danube.
why: Foragers met the first farmers here and some took up their ways.

sources.cite: Borić, D., "The Lepenski Vir conundrum: reinterpretation of the Mesolithic and Neolithic sequences in the Danube Gorges", Antiquity 76, 1026-1039 (2002)

name: Nabta Playa
what: Cattle burials and a stone circle by a seasonal lake in what is now the Egyptian desert.
why: Herders of the Green Sahara; when the rains failed they moved toward the Nile.

sources.cite: Malville, J. M. et al., "Megaliths and Neolithic astronomy in southern Egypt", Nature 392, 488-491 (1998)
